extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent practitioners handling design patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how restriction requirements under 35 U.S.C. 121 apply in design patent applications, including criteria for patentable distinctness/indistinctness of embodiments, reply/election and traversal procedures, telephone provisional elections, and double patenting considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction required to patentably distinct groups (35 U.S.C. 121)
rubrics_metrics.description: Restriction is required under 35 U.S.C. 121 to one of the identified patentably distinct groups of designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reply to such a requirement must include an election of a single group for prosecution on the merits, even if the requirement is traversed (37 CFR 1.143). Any reply that does not include election of a single group will be held nonresponsive. Applicant is also requested to direct cancellation of all drawing figures and the corresponding descriptions which are directed to the nonelected groups. Action on the merits is deferred pending compliance with the requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for patentable indistinctness (overall appearance / minor differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple embodiments of a single inventive concept may be included in the same design application only if they are patentably indistinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embodiments have overall appearances that are basically the same and the differences between them are considered minor and patentably indistinct, or are shown to be obvious in view of analogous prior art cited. If the differences are not minor or are not shown to be obvious, the embodiments are patentably distinct and must be restricted. Relevant case law: In re Rubinfield, In re Platner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness requirement for indistinctness (no analogous prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: To retain multiple embodiments in one application, differences in scope must be minor and the embodiments must be obvious over each other under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) without the aid of analogous prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the difference in scope impacts overall appearance so as to distinguish one embodiment over another, restriction is necessary. The determination that the designs are not patentable over each other (i.e., are obvious variations) supports retention in a single application (Blumcraft, In re Rubinfield).

rubrics_metrics.name: Design claim covers whole design (not parts) — combination/subcombination rule
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim covers the entire design as a whole and does not extend to any individual part or portion thereof; patent protection does not extend to patentably distinct segregable parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combination/subcombination subject matter that is patentably distinct must be supported by separate claims; because only a single claim is permissible in a design patent application, patentably distinct combinations/subcombinations require separate applications/claims. See KeyStone Retaining Wall Systems Inc. v. Westrock Inc., Ex parte Sanford, Blumcraft of Pittsburgh v. Ladd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election requirement and cancellation of nonelected matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A reply to a restriction requirement must include a provisional election of one of the enumerated designs; election must be made even though the requirement may be traversed (37 CFR 1.143).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any reply that fails to elect a single group will be held nonresponsive. Applicant is requested to cancel drawing figures and descriptions directed to nonelected groups. If restriction is made final, applicant must cancel the nonelected groups or take timely appropriate action (37 CFR 1.144).

rubrics_metrics.name: Traversal substantive-evidence requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant traverses a restriction requirement on the grounds that groups are not patentably distinct, applicant must present evidence or identify such evidence now of record showing the groups to be obvious variations of one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Traversal alone without explanation will be treated as an election without traverse. A traversal that specifically points out supposed errors requires the examiner to reevaluate the restriction; if maintained it must be repeated and made final in the next Office action and the arguments answered. No application should be allowed on the next Office action where the response includes an election with traverse unless traversal is withdrawn or the examiner withdraws the restriction. See MPEP § 818.03(a), § 821.01.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traversal based on burden-to-search inapplicable for design patents
rubrics_metrics.description: A traversal arguing 'no serious burden' to search the entire application (as in MPEP § 803) is not applicable to design patent applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that embodiments may be searched together cannot preclude restriction if their appearances are patentably distinct, since patentably distinct embodiments cannot be supported by a single formal design claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner explanation requirement for differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must include a brief explanation of the differences between embodiments that render them patentably distinct when issuing a restriction requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraphs and bracketed explanatory text should be used to identify and explain the differences (examples and bracket placeholders provided throughout MPEP paragraphs referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Telephone provisional election and affirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a provisional election is made during a telephone discussion, affirmation of that election should be made by applicant in replying to the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner may withdraw group(s) from further consideration (37 CFR 1.142(b)) as being for nonelected designs; bracketed form text instructs inserting 'with' or 'without' and other details of the telephone interview for the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to traverse implies admission of indistinctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure of applicant to traverse a determination that embodiments comprise a single inventive concept will be considered an admission of lack of patentable distinction between the embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When restriction is not required (designs are patentably indistinct and retained), any rejection of one embodiment over prior art will apply equally to all embodiments. Applicant's silence (no traverse) is treated as acceptance of the indistinctness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common embodiment warning (avoid double patenting)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a common embodiment is included in more than one group because it is patentably indistinct from embodiments in those groups, applicant is advised that if the common embodiment is elected in this application it should not be included in any continuing application to avoid double patenting under 35 U.S.C. 171 in the new application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide qualifying statement when common embodiment appears in multiple groups to give applicant broadest choices in election while warning of double patenting risk in continuing applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures for groups withdrawn / cancellation of nonelected groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs are provided to notify applicant that nonelected inventions are withdrawn from consideration or must be canceled depending on whether traverse was filed and the stage of prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Groups withdrawn after traverse (37 CFR 1.142(b)); Groups withdrawn without traverse (election made without traverse); Cancellation of nonelected groups where application is otherwise in condition for allowance except for presence of nonelected group — such groups may be canceled without right to petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting determinations and rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Two types of double patenting rejections: (1) 'same invention' statutory double patenting under 35 U.S.C. 171 (same design claimed twice), and (2) nonstatutory double patenting (judicial doctrine) to prevent prolongation of patent term where claims in a second patent are not patentably distinct from claims in a first patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination involves: Is the same design being claimed twice? If yes, apply 35 U.S.C. 171 rejection. If not, are the designs patentably indistinct variations of the same inventive concept? If yes, apply nonstatutory double patenting (obviousness-based) rejection. Double patenting rejections are based on comparison of claims; in design-versus-utility comparisons examiners must be able to recreate the design claimed from the utility claims without reliance on drawings. See MPEP § 804 for procedure charts and case law references.
